title: The Annunciation (25 March)
hook: nine months before Christmas, the Word takes flesh

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saint Joseph, who never says a word in the Gospels. Your line was the silent saint. What good thing did you do without mentioning it? Day six hundred fifty-six.

Count back nine months from December 25. You land on March 25. The Church did that math centuries ago, and so in the middle of Lent, with purple on the altar and Easter still weeks off, there's a sudden white solemnity. Christmas, seen from the beginning. In old Europe, bells in villages rang three times a day, at dawn, at noon and at dusk, and farmers in the fields stopped and bowed their heads to remember this exact moment. Some churches still ring them. Today, the moment the bells remember.
screen: `NINE MONTHS BEFORE CHRISTMAS.` → `WHITE IN THE MIDDLE OF LENT.` → `BELLS AT DAWN, NOON, DUSK.`

segments.voice: Luke sets it in Nazareth, a village nobody expected anything from. The angel Gabriel comes to a young woman, betrothed to Joseph, and greets her: hail, full of grace. He tells her she will conceive a son, and call him Jesus, and he will be called the Son of the Most High. Mary doesn't simply nod. She asks a real question, in the Douay-Rheims: "How shall this be done, because I know not man?" The angel answers that the Holy Spirit will come upon her, and the power of the Most High will overshadow her. He tells her that her old cousin Elizabeth, called barren, is six months pregnant. "Because no word shall be impossible with God." And then Mary's answer, the hinge of the whole story: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word." In Latin, the first word of that last phrase is fiat, let it be done. Catholics often call this Mary's fiat. It's not passive. She asked, she listened, and she chose. Christians believe that in that moment the Word, who in John's gospel was there in the beginning, took flesh in her. That's why, at Mass today, people kneel at the words of the Creed about the incarnation, just as they do on Christmas. And that's what the bells were for. The Angelus, rung morning, noon and evening, walks through this scene in three short lines with a Hail Mary after each: the angel's message, Mary's be it done, and the Word made flesh. A whole Christmas, three times a day, in less than two minutes.
screen: `GABRIEL IN NAZARETH.` · `HOW SHALL THIS BE DONE?` · `NO WORD IMPOSSIBLE WITH GOD.` · `FIAT: LET IT BE DONE.` · then, large: `BE IT DONE TO ME ACCORDING TO THY WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the Angelus, or its shape. If you pray and know it, pray the Angelus now: the three short verses, each followed by a Hail Mary. If you don't know it, let its shape guide the sit. First breath, a message arrives. Second breath, a question is asked. Third breath, a yes is given. Then sit with something you've been asked to carry that you didn't plan. A job, a person, a change. Hold it, and ask whether a yes is possible. The bell holds the time.
The Annunciation. The angel Gabriel's message to Mary, and her yes, kept on March 25, nine months before Christmas. Today's word.
Your line: be it done. Today, at noon, wherever you are, stop for ten seconds and remember the moment in Nazareth. Day six hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: Catholics keep March 25 as the Solemnity of the Annunciation of the Lord (moved when it falls in Holy Week or the Easter octave), kneel at the Creed's words on the incarnation, and many pray the Angelus at 6 a.m., noon and 6 p.m.

original.note: Latin: let it be done, the first word of Mary's answer in the Vulgate (Luke 1:38).

trapdoor: what you thought: the Annunciation is a painting of an angel and a lily.
what it means: the moment Mary said yes, and Christians believe the Word took flesh, nine months before Christmas.
what a scholar hears: the Vulgate's 'fiat mihi secundum verbum tuum'; March 25 was fixed by counting back from December 25, and the Angelus compresses Luke 1 and John 1:14.

notes: The Angelus is described, not quoted. Confirm the description (three versicles, each followed by a Hail Mary, and a closing prayer not mentioned).

Historical relation between the dates of March 25 and December 25 is debated (some argue Christmas was counted from March 25, not the reverse). Script says 'The Church did that math', which is neutral; trapdoor says 'fixed by counting back'. Keeper may prefer softer wording.
Kneeling at the incarnation in the Creed on the Annunciation (GIRM 137). Confirm.
Transfer rule when March 25 falls in Holy Week or the Easter Octave. Confirm.
